title: Evaluation Report on Large Language Models Solving High School Mathematics Questions
extended_summary:
This report evaluates how large language models (LLMs) perform on high school mathematics exam questions and considers their potential use in education. The paper is framed around a performance evaluation problem: whether LLMs can solve representative secondary-school mathematics items accurately, quickly, and with sound reasoning, and whether they can generate multiple valid solution paths.

The approach uses mathematics questions from college entrance examinations spanning 2019–2023 as the evaluation set. The authors test at least eight LLM APIs/models, including domestic and international systems such as GLM-4-Flash, ERNIE-Speed-128K, Spark Lite, Hunyuan-lite, Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, gemma-2-9b-it, Meta-Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, and Yi-34B. They assess single-solution and multi-solution outputs using measures of accuracy, response time, logical reasoning, guidance responsiveness, richness, and solution complexity. The paper also varies prompts to examine whether role-based guidance (e.g., mathematician, student, teacher) changes performance.

The context is high school science/mathematics education in China, using exam-style problems from national college entrance examinations as the benchmark tasks. The population is therefore high school learners, although no student participants are directly involved because the study is a model-benchmark evaluation rather than a classroom intervention. The results suggest meaningful variation across models: some models are faster, some more accurate, and others stronger in logical reasoning or creative multi-solution generation.

Overall, the report concludes that LLMs already show promise for educational use, especially in automated problem solving and guided assistance, but they still need improvement in logical reasoning and creative problem solving. The authors argue that prompt design, model training, and algorithmic optimization could improve educational usefulness, and they suggest future work on other science subjects such as biology and physics.
quality_tier_rationale: This is a grey-literature style evaluation report rather than a peer-reviewed experimental study, and it does not report a clearly controlled design, random assignment, or inferential statistics. The methods are primarily benchmark-style comparisons of model outputs on exam questions.
impact_tier_rationale: The paper suggests potentially meaningful performance differences among LLMs for math problem solving, but the evidence is descriptive and the absolute performance levels are mixed and often modest. It implies possible educational utility, yet the impact on K-12 learning outcomes is indirect and unproven.

interventions.use_case: Benchmarking general-purpose large language models on high school mathematics exam questions, including single-answer and multi-solution prompting to assess their tutoring/problem-solving potential in education.

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports heterogeneous math-performance results across eight LLMs on high school mathematics exam questions (2019-2023). Accuracy was modest overall, with the best single-solution comprehensive-question accuracies reaching 0.95 for ERNIE-Speed-128K and 0.85 for Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, while multiple-choice accuracy ranged from 0.10 to 0.20 and fill-in-the-blank accuracy from 0.10 to 0.25. In the multi-solution setting, Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct achieved the highest correctness rate (0.64), followed closely by ERNIE-Speed-128K (0.63).
finding.measure: Accuracy on multiple-choice, fill-in-the-blank, comprehensive questions; multi-solution correctness rate on high school mathematics exam problems

finding.finding_summary: The report explicitly evaluated logical reasoning and creativity as core performance dimensions of the LLMs. Logic scores were low-to-moderate overall (e.g., 0.28-0.42 in the weighted table), with Hunyuan-lite scoring highest on logic (0.42) and Meta-Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct lowest among the listed models (0.28), while creativity-related complexity scores ranged from 33 to 68, favoring GLM-4-Flash and gemma-2-9b-it. These results suggest that some models can produce multiple solutions and structured reasoning, but reasoning quality remains inconsistent.
finding.measure: Logical reasoning score, guidance attempts/success, and creativity metrics (complexity, richness) in multi-solution math problem solving

finding.finding_summary: The paper finds substantial differences in response time across models and problem formats. In single-solution tasks, the fastest models were typically Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct and gemma-2-9b-it on easier items (e.g., 0.32-0.57 s for some formats), while Yi-34B and especially GLM-4-Flash were much slower on some tasks (e.g., 10.31 s and 16.01 s on question-and-answer tasks; 18.56 s on hard items for GLM-4-Flash). In multi-solution tasks, Spark-lite was fastest (688 s total) and GLM-4-Flash slowest (7400 s), indicating a clear efficiency tradeoff across models.
finding.measure: Response time for single-solution and multi-solution math question answering
